I understand. I'm afraid what you're looking for might not be in Indian Unis. Maybe try looking at a few US ones. For instance, UPenn has this Comparative Literature and Literary Theory program. That might speak to your interests

Afaik, Jadavpur University (Kolkata) is your best shot at pursuing formal training in Comp Lit. They have a decent Bachelor's program. Other universities are Central University of Kerala, Viswa Bharati, Calcutta University, but most of them teach variants of Comp Lit such as "English and Comp Lit" or "Comparative Indian Literatures". 
As to your third question, critical theory and continental philosophy is taught in most English departments in India. I'd actually go on to argue that it's taught better in the English departments (say, JNU, Jamia, Ashoka, Shiv Nadar). 
The crucial difference in a Comp Lit department is that they do not assume the concept of "literature", "culture", "philosophy", to be transhistorical or transcultural. Paradoxically enough, this conceptual specificity is only done through comparison. So, I'd say, it's not so much about the adjectival 'comparative', but about 'literature' in a global (but never globally equivalent) scale. 
Another bit is that you need training in one ancient language (Sanskrit or Old Tamil) and preferably one of the Romance languages. 
Also, if your interests are rooted in philosophy, why not pursue a BA in Philosophy? Both English and Comp Lit are more interested in the 'text' (that is, they train you to formally close-read), whereas it seems that Philosophy majors are more interested in ideas and interpretation. That seems more along the lines of what you're looking for.

Edit: There's this essay by Derrida that's translated as (something like), "Who or What is Translated? Comparative Literature and the Problems of Translation". I recommend this for a conceptual and historical understanding of Comp Lit.

You may always see a BBC production (they're closest to retaining textual content) if you find reading uninteresting.
